concepts.name: Credit risk and PD / LGD / EAD
concepts.definition: Credit risk is the risk of loss from a fall in a credit asset's value because the obligor fails to pay or its creditworthiness worsens. Every topic in the chapter changes, measures or uses PD (probability of default), LGD (loss given default) or EAD (exposure at default). Components: default risk (PD), security risk (collateral can't cover the loss: LGD) and credit-quality risk (value moves with ratings, e.g. a downgrade).
misconceptions: Thinking default is the only credit event: a downgrade with every coupon paid is still a real loss because the required spread widens
Mixing up which risk component maps to PD vs LGD

cards.front: PD, LGD, EAD: what question does each answer?
cards.back: PD: how likely is default? LGD: how much do we lose if they default (what don't we recover)? EAD: how much is owed at the moment of default?

cards.front: Three components of credit risk
cards.back: Default risk (obligor fails to pay, incl. cross-default → PD); Security risk (collateral can't cover the loss → LGD); Credit-quality risk (value moves as credit quality changes, e.g. downgrade; can be gains or losses).

cards.front: Modern view of a credit event
cards.back: Default isn't the only one. A downgrade A → BBB with all coupons paid widens the required spread, so the bond's value falls: a real loss with zero default.

questions.prompt: A bond is downgraded from A to BBB. The issuer continues to pay every coupon on time. Under the modern view of credit risk, the bondholder has:
options: No credit loss, because there has been no default
A credit loss, because the market now requires a wider spread so the bond's value falls
A gain, because the higher spread means higher coupons
An interest rate risk loss, not a credit risk loss
questions.explanation: Credit-quality risk: the downgrade widens the required spread, so the bond's market value drops. That's a real loss even though nothing has defaulted.
feedback: This is the old view, where default was the only credit event. The notes stress it isn't.
The coupon on an existing bond is fixed. A wider required spread lowers the price; it doesn't raise the coupon.
The cause is the issuer's creditworthiness, not a market-wide rate move, so it's credit (credit-quality) risk.

questions.prompt: The collateral backing a defaulted loan sells for less than the amount owed. Which component of credit risk has materialised, and which parameter does it affect?
questions.explanation: Security risk is the risk that the security supporting the asset can't cover the loss, which shows up in LGD (how much is lost once default has happened).
feedback: Default has already happened here; the question is how much is lost, not whether default occurs.
Credit-quality risk is about value moving with ratings, and EAD is the amount owed, not the shortfall on collateral.
Collateral doesn't change whether the borrower defaults in this scenario; it changes how much you lose afterwards.

steps.hint: Multiply all three; express PD and LGD as decimals.
steps.misconception: Using recovery (60%) instead of LGD (40%) gives $36,000.

feedback: That uses the 55% recovery rate instead of the 45% LGD.
That's LGD × EAD: the loss IF default happens, not the expected loss.
That's PD × EAD, which assumes nothing is recovered.

questions.prompt: What does LGD (loss given default) measure?
options: The share of the exposure the bank loses if the borrower defaults
The probability that the borrower defaults
The amount owed at the moment of default
The fall in a loan's value after a credit downgrade
questions.explanation: LGD is how much is lost once default has happened, after whatever is recovered from security. It reflects security risk: the security may not cover the loss.
feedback: That's PD.
That's EAD.
That's credit-quality risk, which can cause losses without any default.

questions.prompt: A borrower's collateral falls in value. As its business struggles, it draws down the rest of its credit line. Which credit risk parameters rise?
options: PD, LGD and EAD all rise
LGD and EAD rise, but PD is unaffected
questions.explanation: Struggling business → higher PD. Weaker collateral → less recovered, so higher LGD. Drawing down the line → more owed at default, so higher EAD. All three move together, which is why EL = PD × LGD × EAD can jump sharply in a downturn.
feedback: The weaker collateral and the extra drawdown also raise LGD and EAD.
The drawdown raises EAD and the business trouble raises PD.
A struggling borrower is more likely to default, so PD rises too.

questions.prompt: Define credit risk.
key_points: A loss from a fall in the value of a credit asset
Because the obligor fails to pay (default)
Or because the obligor's creditworthiness deteriorates (e.g. a downgrade)
questions.model_answer: Credit risk is the risk of loss from a decline in the value of a credit asset, either because the obligor fails to meet its obligations (default) or because its creditworthiness deteriorates, such as a downgrade.
questions.explanation: Credit risk is the risk of loss from a decline in the value of a credit asset, either because the obligor fails to meet its obligations (default) or because its creditworthiness deteriorates, such as a downgrade.

questions.explanation: Loss given default (LGD): what isn't recovered after default.

questions.explanation: Default is only the final stage; deteriorating creditworthiness also reduces a credit asset's value.

questions.prompt: Expected loss = PD × ___ × EAD
questions.explanation: EL = PD × LGD × EAD: how likely default is, how much is lost if it happens, and how much is owed.

questions.prompt: A borrower is downgraded but keeps paying every coupon on time. What happens to the market value of its bonds?
questions.explanation: The market now requires a wider spread, so the bond's value falls: a credit loss without any default.
feedback: A downgrade widens the required spread, which lowers the price.
That's the old default-only view; modern approaches count credit-quality changes too.

questions.prompt: If PD doubles while LGD and EAD stay the same, what happens to expected loss?
questions.explanation: EL is proportional to PD, so doubling PD doubles EL.
feedback: PD is in the numerator of nothing here: EL rises with PD.
Only one term doubled.
EL depends directly on PD.

questions.prompt: In a recession, PD doubles and LGD rises from 40% to 60%, while EAD is unchanged. Expected loss is multiplied by:
questions.explanation: EL scales with both: 2 × (60/40) = 2 × 1.5 = 3. Several parameters moving together is why losses jump in downturns.
feedback: That only counts the change in PD.
That adds the multipliers (2 + 1.5); they multiply.
That only counts the change in LGD.

questions.prompt: A recession hits a bank's business loan book. Trace the combined effect on expected loss (EL = PD × LGD × EAD).
options: EL rises more than PD alone suggests: defaults rise, collateral values fall (LGD ↑) and stressed borrowers draw down credit lines (EAD ↑)
Only PD rises, so EL rises in proportion to PD
EL is unchanged until loans actually default
EL falls because banks stop lending
questions.explanation: Recession → PD ↑ (cycle) · collateral ↓ → LGD ↑ · drawdowns → EAD ↑. The three multiply, so EL can jump sharply.
feedback: LGD and EAD move too, and the effects multiply.
Expected loss is forward-looking; it rises before defaults happen.
Existing loans still carry the higher risk.

concepts.name: Why credit risk matters: NPLs and the cycle
concepts.definition: Credit risk is cyclical: NPLs stay low in good times and jump in recessions. Losses are built in booms (low NPLs tempt lenders to relax standards) and show up in busts. NPLs are a lagging indicator, flow through to provisions (reducing earnings and capital), differ by loan type (real estate swings most, peaking near 8%) and by crisis industry, so concentration is dangerous. Australia's NPLs peaked around 2% after the GFC, far below the US.
misconceptions: Reading low NPLs as a sign credit risk is low going forward
Treating NPLs as a leading indicator

cards.front: Why are NPLs a lagging indicator?
cards.back: A loan only becomes non-performing after the borrower is already in trouble. Pair NPLs with forward-looking measures: early delinquencies, credit spreads and PD estimates.

cards.front: 'Losses are built in booms and show up in busts' — explain
cards.back: In a boom NPLs are low, so lenders relax standards and bring in weaker borrowers. When the economy turns those borrowers can't pay and defaults spike. The low point comes just before the spike.

cards.front: Which loan type's NPLs swing the most?
cards.back: Real estate (peaking near 8%); business and personal loans swing less.

questions.prompt: NPLs have been at historic lows for three years. Which conclusion is most consistent with the course material?
options: Credit risk is low, so standards can safely be relaxed
Losses may be building: low NPLs tempt lenders to loosen standards, and defaults spike when the cycle turns
Real estate lending is now the safest category
questions.explanation: Losses are built in booms and show up in busts. The low point in NPLs comes just before the spike, and NPLs lag, so they say little about what's coming.
feedback: This is exactly the boom-time reasoning the notes warn about.
Backward-looking provisioning left banks under-reserved going into the GFC; this is the mistake expected-loss models were meant to fix.
Real estate NPLs swing the most over the cycle, so low current NPLs don't make it the safest.

questions.prompt: Why is concentrating lending in a single sector dangerous?
options: Because diversified portfolios have higher PD
Because each crisis hits a different industry (real estate late 1980s, telecom/tech around 2000, mortgages 2007–08)
Because sector loans have no collateral
questions.explanation: Each crisis has centred on a different industry, so a portfolio concentrated in one sector can be hit all at once.
feedback: Diversification lowers, not raises, portfolio risk.
Not the reason given; the reason is crisis history.
Collateral isn't the issue; correlated defaults are.

questions.prompt: Explain why NPLs are described as a lagging indicator, and what a bank should use alongside them.
key_points: A loan only becomes non-performing after the borrower is already in trouble
So NPLs confirm losses after the fact rather than predicting them
Use forward-looking measures alongside: early delinquencies, credit spreads, PD estimates
Backward-looking provisioning left banks under-reserved in the GFC, driving the shift to expected-loss models

questions.prompt: How do rising NPLs affect a bank's financial statements?
options: They flow through to provisions, which reduce earnings and capital
They reduce the bank's cost of funds
questions.explanation: NPLs are where credit risk turns into losses: they flow through to provisions, reducing earnings and capital.
feedback: Non-performing loans aren't paying interest.
NPLs are on-balance-sheet loans.
If anything, a weaker bank pays more for funds.
questions.source_note: Slide 6 covers credit quality over the cycle; NPLs feed provisions, which reduce earnings and capital.

questions.prompt: Backward-looking provisioning based on NPLs left banks under-reserved going into the GFC. Which change best addresses this?
options: Provision on expected losses using forward-looking signals such as early delinquencies, credit spreads and PD estimates
Raise provisions only once NPLs start rising
Use a longer history of NPLs
Only lend to sectors whose NPLs are currently low
questions.explanation: NPLs lag: a loan only becomes non-performing after the borrower is already in trouble, and losses are built during booms when NPLs look low. Forward-looking, expected-loss provisioning reserves before the losses show up.
feedback: That's the backward-looking approach that failed: by the time NPLs rise, losses are already locked in.
More history is still backward-looking.
Low current NPLs are exactly when losses are being built.

questions.prompt: Name the concept: loans that have stopped performing; a lagging indicator that confirms credit losses only after borrowers are in trouble.
questions.explanation: Non-performing loans (NPLs) lag: pair them with forward-looking measures like early delinquencies and spreads.

questions.prompt: Credit losses are built in ___ and show up in ___.
questions.explanation: Low NPLs in a boom tempt lenders to loosen standards; those weaker loans default when the economy turns.

questions.prompt: What tends to happen to lending standards after NPLs have stayed low for a long time?
options: They loosen and weaker borrowers are let in
questions.explanation: Lenders read low NPLs as a sign they can relax standards and compete for market share.
feedback: Tightening happens after losses appear, not during the boom.
Standards move with the cycle.
Lending usually grows in a boom.

questions.prompt: Lenders loosen standards during a boom, then the economy turns down. What happens to NPLs, and why?
options: They jump: weaker borrowers admitted in the boom can't pay once the cycle turns
They fall, because standards were loosened
Nothing, because NPLs only reflect current lending
They rose already during the boom
questions.explanation: Boom → looser standards → weaker borrowers → defaults spike in the downturn. The low point in NPLs comes just before the spike.
feedback: Looser standards add risk; it shows up later.
NPLs reflect loans made earlier, including the boom's weaker loans.
NPLs are lowest during the boom; that's what tempts lenders.

concepts.name: Loan structure and PD (maturity, fixed vs floating)
concepts.definition: How a loan is structured changes the borrower's likelihood of default. Longer maturity gives more time for credit quality to deteriorate, so higher PD. Switching from fixed to floating moves interest rate risk from the bank to the borrower, but higher repayments when rates rise raise PD, so it comes back to the bank as credit risk. The bank never gets rid of the risk; it only changes form. Real estate: long maturities, investor lending riskier than owner-occupier, ARMs raise PD when rates rise.
misconceptions: Saying a floating rate shifts credit risk to the borrower (credit risk always sits with the lender)
Treating maturity and duration as the same thing: maturity is a PD idea, duration is a value idea (used in RAROC)
Thinking owner-occupier lending is riskier than investor lending

cards.front: Fixed vs floating: who bears interest rate risk and credit risk?
cards.back: Fixed: IR risk → bank; credit risk → bank. Floating: IR risk → borrower; credit risk → bank (always). Rising repayments raise PD, so the risk bounces back as credit risk.

cards.front: Maturity vs duration in credit risk
cards.back: Maturity is a PD idea (more time for things to go wrong). Duration is a value idea used in RAROC (how much the loan's value drops when the risk premium rises). Long loans usually have both, but they answer different questions.

cards.front: Why is investor property lending riskier than owner-occupier?
cards.back: An investor faces a purely financial decision, so if the property falls in value they're more willing to walk away. An owner-occupier is also protecting their home.

questions.prompt: A bank switches its business loans from fixed to floating rates. Which statement is correct?
options: The bank removes both interest rate risk and credit risk
Interest rate risk shifts to the borrower, and credit risk shifts to the borrower too
Interest rate risk shifts to the borrower, but rising repayments raise PD, so the bank's credit risk rises
Interest rate risk stays with the bank; only credit risk changes
questions.explanation: The risk changes form rather than disappearing: the borrower carries the rate risk, higher repayments push up default probability, and credit risk always sits with whoever is owed the money, i.e. the bank.
feedback: The bank never gets rid of the risk; it only changes form.
Credit risk is the risk the other side doesn't pay, so it always sits with the lender. The borrower owes the bank, so it can't bear credit risk on this loan.
Under a floating rate the borrower's repayments move with market rates, so the rate risk does move to them.

questions.prompt: Why does a longer loan maturity raise PD?
options: Because the loan's duration is higher, so its value is more sensitive to rates
Because there is more time for the borrower's credit quality to deteriorate
Because long loans always carry floating rates
Because long loans have higher LGD
questions.explanation: Maturity is a PD idea: more time for things to go wrong.
feedback: That's duration, a value idea used in RAROC. The notes flag this as a classic trap.
Maturity and the rate type are separate choices.
LGD is about recovery after default, not the likelihood of default.

questions.prompt: Explain why switching a loan from fixed to floating rate doesn't remove the bank's risk.
key_points: Floating rate moves interest rate risk from the bank to the borrower
When rates rise, the borrower's repayments rise
Higher repayments raise the borrower's probability of default
Credit risk always stays with the bank (the lender)
So the risk changes form from interest rate risk to credit risk rather than disappearing

options: The owner-occupier, because they have less income

Same loan, different incentives.

Risk falls, because investors are less likely to default than owner-occupiers

feedback: The risk only changes form: it returns as credit risk, which always sits with the lender.
Rising ARM repayments push PD up as well.
Investor lending is riskier, not safer.

questions.prompt: Under a floating rate, interest rate risk is borne by the ___, but credit risk is always borne by the ___.
questions.explanation: Credit risk sits with whoever is owed the money. A floating rate shifts rate risk to the borrower, but it returns as credit risk.

questions.prompt: Name the concept: a mortgage whose interest rate resets with market rates, so repayments rise when rates rise.
questions.explanation: An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM): rising rates raise repayments and so PD.

questions.prompt: A loan's maturity is lengthened. What happens to its PD?
questions.explanation: Longer maturity gives credit quality more time to deteriorate, so PD rises.
feedback: More time means more chance of deterioration, not less.
Maturity is one of the drivers of PD.

questions.prompt: How does maturity differ from duration as a driver of credit risk?
options: Maturity is a PD idea (more time for things to go wrong); duration is a value idea (how much the loan's value falls when the risk premium rises)
Maturity drives LGD; duration drives EAD
Duration is a PD idea; maturity is a value idea
questions.explanation: A long loan usually has both a higher PD and a bigger value drop, but they answer different questions. Duration is what RAROC uses.
feedback: They're related but measure different things.
Neither is mainly about LGD or EAD.
That's the wrong way round.

questions.prompt: Rates rise on a book of adjustable-rate mortgages. What happens to the bank's credit risk?
options: Increases: higher repayments raise borrowers' PD
Decreases: borrowers now carry the interest rate risk
No change: credit risk doesn't depend on rates
Decreases: higher rates mean more interest income

feedback: That's the first step only; it bounces back as credit risk.
Repayment burdens drive PD.

questions.prompt: Switching from fixed to floating moves interest rate risk to the ___, but higher repayments raise the ___, so the risk returns to the bank as credit risk.
questions.explanation: Rate risk to the borrower → repayments ↑ → PD ↑ → credit risk for the bank.

concepts.name: LGD: order of repayment
concepts.definition: LGD answers 'what do we get back if they don't pay?'. Order of repayment in default: (1) secured/senior lenders, paid first from sale of the specific collateral; (2) unsecured/junior lenders, a claim on the borrower drawn from the common pool (cash, inventory, unpledged equipment, surplus after secured lenders); (3) subordinated debt, paid only after unsecured lenders are paid in full; (4) shareholders, the residual, usually nothing. Risk and return both rise down the list: the later you're paid, the higher LGD and the higher the expected return.
misconceptions: Putting subordinated debt ahead of unsecured lenders
Thinking secured lenders' collateral goes into the common pool

cards.front: Order of repayment in default
cards.back: 1. Secured (senior), from the specific collateral. 2. Unsecured (junior), from the common pool. 3. Subordinated debt, after unsecured are paid in full. 4. Shareholders, residual (usually nothing).

cards.front: What's in the unsecured lenders' common pool?
cards.back: Cash, inventory, unpledged equipment, plus any surplus left after secured lenders are paid from their collateral.

cards.front: How do LGD and expected return move down the repayment order?
cards.back: Both rise. The later you're paid, the less you expect to recover (higher LGD), so you demand a higher expected return.

questions.prompt: A firm defaults. Its collateral sells for more than the secured loan. Where does the surplus go?
options: To the secured lender as a bonus
Into the common pool for unsecured lenders
questions.explanation: Secured lenders are paid from their collateral; any surplus joins cash, inventory and unpledged equipment in the common pool for unsecured lenders.
feedback: Secured lenders recover up to what they're owed, no more.
Subordinated holders are only paid after unsecured lenders are paid in full.
Shareholders are last; they only get what's left after all lenders.

questions.prompt: Rank from LOWEST to HIGHEST expected LGD:
options: Subordinated debt, unsecured loan, secured loan
Secured loan, unsecured loan, subordinated debt
Unsecured loan, secured loan, subordinated debt
Secured loan, subordinated debt, unsecured loan
questions.explanation: Secured lenders are paid first (lowest LGD), then unsecured, then subordinated (highest LGD of the lenders).
feedback: This is highest to lowest.
Secured lenders recover first, so they have the lowest LGD.
Subordinated debt is paid after unsecured lenders, so it has higher LGD than them.

questions.prompt: Why do subordinated debt holders demand a higher expected return than unsecured lenders to the same firm?
options: They're paid only after unsecured lenders are paid in full, so they expect to recover less (higher LGD)
They have a claim on specific collateral
questions.explanation: Risk and return both rise down the repayment order: later payment means lower expected recovery, so a higher required return.
feedback: Maturity isn't what separates them in the repayment order.
That describes secured lenders.
They bear more credit risk, not less.

questions.prompt: A firm defaults. Its plant, pledged to a $60m secured loan, sells for $70m. Its other assets (cash, inventory, unpledged equipment) raise $20m. Unsecured lenders are owed $50m and subordinated debt holders $30m. What is the unsecured lenders' LGD?
questions.explanation: Secured lender takes $60m; the $10m surplus joins the $20m common pool = $30m. Unsecured lenders recover $30m of $50m (60%), so LGD = 40%. Subordinated holders get nothing.
feedback: 60% is the recovery rate, not LGD (or the LGD if you forgot the $10m surplus from the plant).
That splits the pool with subordinated debt, but subordinated holders are paid only after unsecured lenders are paid in full.

questions.prompt: Name the concept: a loan backed by a first claim on specific assets of the borrower.
questions.explanation: A secured (asset-backed) loan is repaid first from the sale of its collateral.

questions.prompt: An unsecured loan, also called ___ debt, has only a general claim on the borrower.
questions.explanation: Unsecured (junior) lenders share a common pool after secured lenders are paid.

questions.prompt: A lender moves from a secured loan to subordinated debt in the same firm. What happens to its expected LGD?
questions.explanation: Subordinated debt is paid after secured and unsecured lenders, so less is recovered: LGD rises.
feedback: Lower in the repayment order means less recovered.
Seniority is the main driver of LGD.

questions.prompt: How does a secured loan differ from an unsecured loan?
options: Secured: a first claim on specific assets; unsecured: only a general claim on the borrower
Secured loans always have a higher PD
Unsecured lenders are paid first in a default
There's no difference once the borrower defaults
questions.explanation: Security changes how much is recovered (LGD), not whether the borrower defaults.
feedback: Security affects recovery, not the likelihood of default.
Secured lenders are paid first.
Default is exactly when the difference matters.

questions.prompt: Collateral values fall across the economy. What happens to recoveries for secured lenders and for unsecured lenders to the same firms?
options: Both fall: secured lenders recover less from their collateral, and there's less surplus left for unsecured lenders' common pool
Neither changes, because seniority is unchanged
questions.explanation: Collateral ↓ → secured recoveries ↓ → surplus to common pool ↓ → unsecured recoveries ↓. LGD rises down the whole order.
feedback: Any collateral surplus also flows to unsecured lenders, so they lose it too.

concepts.name: Loan-to-value (LTV) and the security buffer
concepts.definition: LTV = Loan / Property value. The bank's security buffer is the borrower's equity: Property value − Loan = (1 − LTV) × Property value, i.e. how far prices can fall before a forced sale stops covering the loan. LTV works from two sides: for the borrower it's their stake (high LTV → higher PD); for the bank it's a cushion (high LTV → higher LGD). Above 100% (negative equity) there's no buffer: PD and LGD both rise.
concepts.formula: Buffer = (1 − LTV) × V;  LTV = L / V
misconceptions: Thinking LTV only affects LGD (it affects PD too, through the borrower's equity stake)
Forgetting that LTV rises when prices fall even though the loan is unchanged

cards.front: Security buffer formula
cards.back: Buffer = Property value − Loan = (1 − LTV) × Property value. It's how far prices can fall before a forced sale stops covering the loan.

cards.front: How does LTV affect PD and LGD?
cards.back: Borrower's side: it's their stake, so high LTV → higher PD (less equity to protect). Bank's side: it's the cushion, so high LTV → higher LGD.

cards.front: What happens above 100% LTV?
cards.back: Negative equity: the borrower owes more than the home is worth (less reason to keep paying → PD up) and the bank takes a loss on sale (LGD up).

From the borrower's side it's their stake: less equity to protect means higher PD
From the bank's side it's a cushion: less cushion means a forced sale may not cover the loan, so higher LGD

steps.ask: Largest % price fall before the buffer is gone

concepts.name: Expected return, k* and credit rationing
concepts.definition: E(1 + r) = p(1 + k) + (1 − p) × 0 = p(1 + k), where p is the probability of repayment and k the contractual rate. concepts.name: Credit spreads and implied PD
concepts.definition: Credit spread C = k − i (risky yield minus risk-free yield of the same maturity). Term structure: spreads rise with maturity, steeply at short maturities then flatter; lower-rated issuers have higher spreads at every maturity. Implied PD: a rational investor sets the expected payoff on the risky asset equal to the risk-free payoff: (1 + i) = p(1 + k), so p = (1 + i)/(1 + k) and PD = 1 − p. With recovery γ: 1 + i = (1 − p)γ(1 + k) + p(1 + k), giving PD(with recovery) = PD(no recovery)/(1 − γ). Adding recovery raises implied PD: if each default costs less, the same market spread must be compensating for more frequent defaults.

concepts.name: RAROC
concepts.definition: RAROC = one-year income on a loan ÷ loan (asset) risk or capital at risk. It compares income with the capital the bank could lose, not the loan's size. Approve if RAROC ≥ the bank's benchmark. Numerator: net income = all-in spread (spread over cost of funds + fees) × loan amount. Denominator: capital at risk from the duration model: ΔL = −D × L × ΔR/(1 + R), where ΔR is the increase in the risk premium under an adverse (e.g. 99th percentile) scenario; RAROC uses the size of the loss. Longer duration = bigger value drop = more capital at risk. To approve a rejected loan: raise income (fees, spread) or reduce risk (shorter duration, smaller loan).

concepts.name: Transferring credit risk: commercial paper
concepts.definition: Commercial paper (CP) is a short-term, unsecured IOU sold by a company directly to investors (usually 30–90 days, max 270). It's disintermediation: the bank is bypassed, the company pays less and investors earn more than on a deposit. Investors who buy the paper bear the default risk, spread across many holders (money market funds, insurers, other firms). Risk stays low because CP is unsecured, so the market only accepts large, highly rated issuers.
